title: What it asks
hookLine: scholars list its conditions: knowledge, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission

cards: A key with no teeth will slide into a lock and turn nothing. Imam al-Bukhari, at the head of a chapter in his collection, records a saying of an early teacher, Wahb ibn Munabbih.
Someone asked him whether la ilaha illallah is the key to Paradise. Yes, he said. But every key has teeth.
Bring a key with its teeth, and the door opens for you. Bring one without, and it won't. So what are the teeth?
Later scholars tried to name them.

teach.b: One list some scholars teach is called the conditions of la ilaha illallah. Not extra rules added on, but what it takes for the words to be more than sound.
First, knowing. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "So know (O Muhammad) that there is no God save Allah." Know, not just repeat: understand what the no and the yes mean.
The Qur'an describes the true believers as those who believe in Allah and His messenger "and afterward doubt not."
Some who teach this list draw a line here: a question passing through the mind isn't the same as doubt that has settled in. Asking is still welcome.
Third, sincerity: saying it for God, not for a marriage, a job, or a crowd's approval.
The Qur'an says people were commanded to serve Allah "keeping religion pure for Him." Pure there means unmixed, said for one audience.

Then the rest of the list: truthfulness, so the tongue and the heart say the same thing; love, for God and for what the words point to; acceptance, taking the whole testimony and not just the comfortable part; and submission, letting it shape what you actually do.

Notice what the list is for. Not to sit in judgment over someone else's shahadah; yesterday's story ruled that out, since no one splits open a heart. It's a mirror, held up by people who wanted to check their own key.

how: Some Muslim teachers explain the shahadah through its conditions, using the list as a way for believers to examine their own faith rather than to judge others'.

practice: Let the list pass slowly through your mind: knowing, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission, and notice which one catches.

Whether you're Muslim or not, you can ask the same of anything you say you stand for: do I know it, am I sure of it, do I mean it? Stay with that one, without grading yourself, and if you pray, ask for help with it.
